⚙️ Under the hood · Step 6 of 8 · 7 min

Tokens, embeddings and attention

Dot products, softmax and why transformers scale as n².

🔤 From text to vectors

A language model never sees letters. The text is cut into tokens (words or pieces of words). Each token has a number, and that number picks a row from a big table of vectors: its embedding.

Training moves these vectors so that tokens used in similar ways end up pointing in similar directions.

Task. The dot product measures how much two vectors point the same way. For a = (1, 2) and b = (3, 1), what is a·b?

Show the solution

1·3 + 2·1 = 5.

📐 Cosine similarity

The dot product also grows with the length of the vectors. Dividing by the lengths leaves only the angle: this is the cosine similarity.

cos(a, b) = a·b / (|a|·|b|)

1 means the same direction, 0 means perpendicular (unrelated), −1 means opposite.

Task. What is the cosine similarity of a = (1, 0) and b = (0, 1)?

Show the solution

a·b = 1·0 + 0·1 = 0, so the cosine is 0: the vectors are perpendicular. For (2, 0) and (5, 0) it would be 1: the same direction, whatever the lengths.

🎚️ Softmax turns scores into probabilities

A model produces a score for every possible next token. Softmax turns the scores into probabilities: all positive, adding up to 1. A higher score gets a bigger share, and the gaps are stretched.

softmax(z_i) = e^(z_i) / Σ_j e^(z_j)

Task. Two tokens have the scores (2, 2). What probability does softmax give to the first one?

Show the solution

Equal scores get equal shares: 0.5. Softmax depends on the differences between the scores, not on their size: (100, 100) also gives 0.5.

Task. Three tokens have the scores (5, 1, 1). Roughly what probability does softmax give to the first one?

Show the answer

Right answer: About 0.96

148.4 / (148.4 + 2.72 + 2.72) ≈ 0.96. A gap of 4 in the scores becomes near certainty. (0.71 would be the plain share 5/7: softmax is far sharper.)

👀 Attention in one line

In a transformer every token asks: which other tokens matter to me? It compares its query vector with the key of every token (dot products), turns those scores into weights with softmax, and takes the weighted average of the tokens' values.

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q·K^T / √d) · V

Task. A sequence has n tokens, and every token attends to every token. How does the number of attention scores grow with n?

Show the answer

Right answer: Like n²

n queries times n keys gives n² scores. Double the context and attention costs four times as much: one reason long contexts are expensive.

Task. A context of 1,000 tokens needs 1 million attention scores in each attention head. How many million does a context of 4,000 tokens need?

Show the solution

4,000² = 16,000,000: sixteen million, which is 16 times more for 4 times the text.

Task. Before softmax, a language model divides its scores by a temperature T. Compared with T = 1, what does T = 0.2 do?

Show the answer

Right answer: It sharpens the distribution: the top token wins more often

Dividing by a small T stretches the gaps between the scores, so softmax concentrates on the top one. A high T flattens the distribution: more surprising text, and more mistakes.

Task. Attention is a weighted average, so by itself it ignores word order. How does a transformer tell “dog bites man” from “man bites dog”?

Show the answer

Right answer: Information about each token's position is added to the model's input

The position has to be injected: as positional encodings added to the embeddings, or as rotations applied inside attention (RoPE).

Remember

  • Text → tokens → numbers → embedding vectors.
  • The dot product and the cosine measure how similar two vectors are.
  • Softmax turns scores into probabilities and depends only on their differences.
  • Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q·K^T / √d) · V, and its cost grows like n².
  • Temperature reshapes the distribution; position has to be added separately.
